questions.q: What is the most accurate formal definition of an algorithm?
o: A programming language used to write software
A sequence of instructions for solving a computational problem
A physical device that processes data
A collection of related data values
questions.e: Formally, an algorithm is a sequence of instructions for solving a computational problem; informally it is a process, method, technique or recipe that takes an input and produces an output.

questions.q: The property of an algorithm that requires it to terminate after a finite amount of time is called what?
o: Definiteness
Finiteness
Effectiveness
Correctness
questions.e: Finiteness requires that an algorithm terminate after a finite amount of time. Definiteness requires clear, unambiguous instructions, and effectiveness requires simple, basic and feasible instructions.

questions.q: Which algorithm feature requires that every instruction be clear and unambiguous?
o: Finiteness
Definiteness
Effectiveness
Valid input
questions.e: Definiteness is the requirement that an algorithm's instructions be clear and unambiguous. Finiteness concerns termination, and effectiveness concerns instructions being simple and feasible.

questions.q: The requirement that an algorithm's instructions be simple, basic and feasible is known as which feature?
o: Finiteness
Definiteness
Effectiveness
Correctness
questions.e: Effectiveness requires that the instructions be simple, basic and feasible to carry out. The other listed features are finiteness (termination) and definiteness (unambiguity).

questions.q: A recursive algorithm is best described as one that does what?
o: Tries all possibilities until a satisfactory solution is found
Calls itself, obtaining the result for the current input from the returned value for a previous input
Divides the problem into subproblems and combines their solutions
Remembers past results to compute new ones
questions.e: A recursive algorithm is one that calls itself, obtaining the result for the current input by applying simple operations to the returned value for the previous input.

questions.q: A brute force algorithm solves a problem in what way?
o: By remembering and reusing past results
By simply trying all possibilities until a satisfactory solution is found, stopping once one is good enough
By always taking the locally best choice at each phase
By transforming the problem into a different one
questions.e: A brute force algorithm simply tries all possibilities until a satisfactory solution is found, stopping as soon as a solution that is good enough is reached.

questions.q: A divide and conquer algorithm consists of which two parts?
o: Sorting the input and then searching it
Dividing the problem into smaller subproblems of the same type solved recursively, then combining their solutions into a solution to the original problem
Guessing a solution and then verifying it
Taking a greedy choice and then backtracking
questions.e: Divide and conquer has two parts: divide the problem into smaller subproblems of the same type and solve these recursively, then combine the subproblem solutions into a solution to the original problem.

questions.q: What characterises a dynamic programming algorithm?
o: It never stores intermediate results
It remembers past results and uses them to find new results, generally for optimization problems
It always picks the nearest option without regard to the future
It tries every possibility exhaustively
questions.e: A dynamic programming algorithm remembers past results and uses them to find new results; it is generally used for optimization problems where multiple solutions exist and the best one must be found.

questions.q: How does a greedy algorithm proceed when solving an optimization problem?
o: It exhaustively tests all candidate solutions
It works in phases, taking the best it can get right now at each phase without regard for future consequences, hoping local optima lead to a global optimum
It stores all previous results in a table
It divides the problem into equal halves
questions.e: A greedy algorithm works in phases; at each phase it takes the best it can get right now, without regard for future consequences, hoping that choosing a local optimum at each step yields a global optimum.

questions.q: What distinguishes a heuristic algorithm from an exact algorithm?
o: It always guarantees the best solution
It finds a solution among all possible ones but does not guarantee the best; it typically finds a near-best solution quickly
It always runs in constant time
It only works on sorted data
questions.e: A heuristic algorithm finds solutions among all possible ones but does not guarantee the best will be found, so it is approximate rather than exact; it usually finds a solution close to the best one quickly and easily.

questions.q: An optimization problem is one in which you want to find what?
o: Any solution that satisfies the constraints
Not just a solution, but the best solution
Only the number of possible solutions
A solution that runs in constant time
questions.e: An optimization problem is one in which you want to find not just a solution but the best solution; greedy and dynamic programming algorithms are often applied to such problems.

questions.q: In the arrayMax algorithm that finds the maximum element of an array A of n integers, with what value is the running maximum initialised before the loop?
o: A[0], the first element
The last element A[n-1]
Negative infinity
questions.e: The arrayMax algorithm sets max to A[0], then iterates i from 1 to n-1, updating max whenever A[i] exceeds it, and finally returns max.

questions.q: What is a search algorithm?
o: An algorithm that sorts items into order
An algorithm for finding an item with specified properties among a collection of items
An algorithm that compresses data
An algorithm that always calls itself
questions.e: A search algorithm is an algorithm for finding an item with specified properties among a collection of items.

questions.q: Which of the following is a general algorithm design paradigm?
o: Compilation
Divide-and-conquer
Tokenization
Serialization
questions.e: General algorithm design paradigms include divide-and-conquer, brute force, incremental, dynamic programming, greedy, and randomized/probabilistic approaches.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of algorithm analysis?
o: To rewrite the algorithm in a different language
To measure an algorithm's efficiency and predict its resource requirements
To find syntax errors in the code
To draw the algorithm's flowchart
questions.e: Algorithm analysis is used to measure an algorithm's efficiency and to predict its resource requirements in terms of time and space, with computation (running) time being the primary concern.

questions.q: Between time and space, which resource is stated to be of primary concern in algorithm analysis?
o: Space (memory)
Computation time (running time)
Disk usage
Network bandwidth
questions.e: While both time and space are resources of interest, computation time (running time) is of primary concern in algorithm analysis.

questions.q: The running time of an algorithm for a given input is defined as which of the following?
o: The number of lines of code in the algorithm
The total number of primitive operations (steps) executed by the algorithm on that input
The number of variables declared
The size of the input alone
questions.e: The running time for a given input is the total number of primitive operations, or steps, executed by the algorithm on that input; it is also called the time complexity of the algorithm.

questions.q: A single simple instruction or memory access counted during analysis is referred to as what?
o: A subroutine
A primitive operation or step
A complexity class
An asymptote
questions.e: Each simple instruction and each access to memory is a primitive operation or step; the running time is the total number of these executed.

questions.q: What are the two main approaches to computing an algorithm's running time?
o: Recursive and iterative
Experimental and theoretical
Best-case and worst-case
Linear and logarithmic
questions.e: The two main approaches to computing running time are the experimental approach (implement and time the program) and the theoretical approach (analyse the algorithm mathematically).

questions.q: In the experimental approach to measuring running time, what is done after writing the program?
o: The algorithm is proven correct by hand
The program is run with inputs of varying size and order, timed accurately, and the results are plotted
The algorithm is converted to pseudocode
The number of variables is counted
questions.e: In the experimental approach, the program is run with inputs of varying size and order, an accurate timing function is used to measure the actual running time, and the results are plotted.

questions.q: Which of the following is a limitation of the experimental approach to measuring algorithm efficiency?
o: It cannot handle recursive algorithms
The measured running time depends on the computer speed, programming language, compiler and program quality
It always overestimates the running time
It requires no implementation
questions.e: The experimental approach requires implementing and testing the algorithm, and the running time then depends on external factors such as the speed of the computer, the programming language, the compiler, and the quality of the program; good analysis should be independent of these.

questions.q: Why is the theoretical approach to analysis preferred over the experimental approach for comparing algorithms?
o: It gives exact millisecond timings
It should be independent of external factors like computer speed, language and compiler
It requires the program to be executed many times
It only works for small inputs
questions.e: Algorithm analysis should be independent of external factors such as computer speed, programming language and compiler; the theoretical approach achieves this, whereas the experimental approach's results depend on those factors.

questions.q: The number of times a basic operation executes is often written as a function C(n). If C(n) = (1/2)n(n-1) and the cost per operation c_op = 1, what is T(n)?
questions.e: The running time estimate is T(n) = c_op * C(n). With c_op = 1 and C(n) = (1/2)n(n-1), T(n) = (1/2)n(n-1).

questions.q: 'Time complexity' of an algorithm is another name for which of the following?
o: The number of variables it uses
Its running time, i.e. the total number of primitive operations executed for a given input
The amount of source code
The number of times it is compiled
questions.e: The running time of an algorithm for a given input — the total number of primitive operations executed — is also referred to as the time complexity of the algorithm.

questions.q: The best-case efficiency of an algorithm corresponds to which kind of input, and how useful is it considered?
o: The input on which it runs longest; the most useful measure
The input on which it runs fastest; not a very useful measure
A random input; the only reliable measure
The largest possible input; always required
questions.e: Best-case efficiency is for the input of size n on which the algorithm runs fastest; it is not a very useful measure, because if even the best case is not good enough you might discard the algorithm.

questions.q: Which case of efficiency analysis is described as the most useful, providing a guarantee that running time will not exceed it for any input of size n?
o: Best case
Worst case
Average case
Random case
questions.e: Worst-case efficiency is for the input on which the algorithm runs longest; it is the most useful measure, is easier to analyse, and guarantees that for any input of size n the time will not exceed it, which is crucial for time-critical applications.

questions.q: Why is average-case efficiency often difficult to determine?
o: Because it equals the worst case
Because it requires a definition of the probability of each input, which is usually difficult to provide and analyse
Because it depends on the compiler used
Because it can only be measured experimentally
questions.e: Average-case efficiency is the average of the running times over all possible inputs of size n; it requires a definition of the probability of each input, which is usually difficult to provide and to analyse.

questions.q: In space complexity, what is the difference between the fixed part and the variable part?
o: The fixed part depends on input size; the variable part does not
The fixed part is space for instructions and data independent of problem size; the variable part is space for variables whose size depends on the problem size
The fixed part is always larger than the variable part
There is no difference
questions.e: Space complexity is the memory required to run to completion. Its fixed part is the space for instructions and data that is independent of problem size, while its variable part is space for variables whose size depends on the size of the problem.

questions.q: For very large inputs, what property of a function is said to really matter when distinguishing efficient algorithms from inefficient ones?
o: Its value on small inputs
Its order (rate) of growth
The number of its terms
Its constant coefficients
questions.e: A difference in running times on small inputs is not what distinguishes efficient from inefficient algorithms; for very large values, only the order of growth of a function counts.

questions.q: A set of problems that all have similar complexity is called what?
o: A design paradigm
A complexity class
An asymptote
A primitive operation
questions.e: A set of problems having similar complexity is called a complexity class.

questions.q: In the standard complexity classes, which running time typically arises in algorithms that must pass through all n elements of the input a constant number of times?
o: Constant, 1
Logarithmic, log n
Linear, n
Quadratic, n^2
questions.e: Linear running time (n) arises when an algorithm is forced to pass through all elements of the input (of size n) a constant number of times. Constant time (1) is a single RAM-model operation, and logarithmic time (log n) arises when a problem is repeatedly reduced to a smaller version.

questions.q: Logarithmic (log n) running time normally occurs in algorithms that do what?
o: Pass through every element a constant number of times
Transform a bigger problem into a smaller version whose input size is a ratio of the original
Perform a single constant-time operation
Examine every pair of elements
questions.e: Logarithmic time normally occurs in algorithms that transform a bigger problem into a smaller version whose input size is a ratio (fraction) of the original problem, such as repeatedly halving it.

questions.q: Which asymptotic notation means 'order at most' and gives a tight upper bound on growth rate?
o: Big Theta (Θ)
Big O
Big Omega (Ω)
Little o
questions.e: Big O means 'order at most' and provides an upper bound on the growth rate. Big Theta (Θ) means 'order exactly' (tight bound) and Big Omega (Ω) means 'order at least' (lower bound).

questions.q: Which asymptotic notation means 'order exactly', giving a tight bound?
o: Big O
Big Theta (Θ)
Big Omega (Ω)
Little o
questions.e: Big Theta (Θ) means 'order exactly' and gives a tight bound; Big O gives an upper bound ('order at most') and Big Omega gives a lower bound ('order at least').

questions.q: By the formal definition, f(n) is O(g(n)) if there exist positive constants c and n0 such that which condition holds?
o: f(n) >= c*g(n) for all n >= n0
f(n) <= c*g(n) for all n >= n0
f(n) = c*g(n) for all n
f(n) < g(n) for all n
questions.e: f(n) is O(g(n)) if there are positive constants c and n0 such that f(n) <= c*g(n) for all n >= n0; g(n) is thus an asymptotic upper bound of f(n).

questions.q: By the formal definition, f(n) is Ω(g(n)) if there exist positive constants c and n0 such that which condition holds?
o: f(n) <= c*g(n) for all n >= n0
f(n) >= c*g(n) for all n >= n0
f(n) = c*g(n) for all n < n0
f(n) < c*g(n) for all n
questions.e: f(n) is Ω(g(n)) if there exist positive constants c and n0 such that f(n) >= c*g(n) for all n >= n0; g(n) is then an asymptotic lower bound of f(n).

questions.q: To show that 2n + 10 is O(n) using f(n) <= c*n, which choice of constants works?
o: c = 1 and n0 = 1
c = 3 and n0 = 10
c = 2 and n0 = 0
c = 10 and n0 = 2
questions.e: For 2n + 10 <= c*n, picking c = 3 and n0 = 10 satisfies the inequality for all n >= n0, so 2n + 10 is O(n).

questions.q: To show that 7n - 2 is O(n), which constants satisfy 7n - 2 <= c*n for all n >= n0?
o: c = 7 and n0 = 2
c = 8 and n0 = 1
c = 1 and n0 = 7
c = 2 and n0 = 8
questions.e: 7n - 2 <= c*n holds for c = 8 and n0 = 1, so 7n - 2 is O(n).

questions.q: The function 3n^3 + 20n^2 + 5 belongs to which order, and with which sample constants?
o: O(n^2), with c = 3 and n0 = 20
O(n^3), with c = 4 and n0 = 21
O(n), with c = 28 and n0 = 1
O(n^4), with c = 1 and n0 = 5
questions.e: 3n^3 + 20n^2 + 5 is O(n^3); it satisfies 3n^3 + 20n^2 + 5 <= c*n^3 for c = 4 and n0 = 21.

questions.q: To prove that f(n) = n^3 is Ω(n^2), which reasoning and constants are used?
o: n^3 <= n^2 for n >= 1, so c = 1 and n0 = 1
n^3 >= n^2 for all n >= 1, so c = 1 and n0 = 1
n^3 = n^2 for n >= 2, so c = 2 and n0 = 2
n^3 < n^2 for n >= 0, so c = 0 and n0 = 0
questions.e: Since n^3 >= n^2 for all n >= 1, the definition of Ω is satisfied with c = 1 and n0 = 1, proving n^3 is Ω(n^2).

questions.q: Informally, the set O(g(n)) contains all functions with which order of growth relative to g(n)?
o: A strictly higher order of growth
A lower or the same order of growth (to within a constant multiple)
Exactly the same order only
An unrelated order of growth
questions.e: Informally, O(g(n)) is the set of all functions with a lower or the same order of growth as g(n), to within a constant multiple, as n goes to infinity; it is an upper bound.

questions.q: Informally, the set Ω(g(n)) contains all functions with which order of growth relative to g(n)?
o: A lower or the same order of growth
A higher or the same order of growth (to within a constant multiple)
Exactly the same order only
A strictly lower order of growth
questions.e: Informally, Ω(g(n)) is the set of all functions with a higher or the same order of growth as g(n), to within a constant multiple, as n goes to infinity; it is a lower bound.

questions.q: Which is stated as a limitation of asymptotic notation?
o: It cannot categorise algorithms by growth rate
It is not always useful for analysis on fixed-size inputs, since all results are for sufficiently large inputs
It requires knowing the exact constants
It only applies to sorting algorithms
questions.e: Asymptotic notation categorises algorithms by growth rate and ignores small constants and small inputs, but a limitation is that it is not always useful for fixed-size inputs, since all results hold only for sufficiently large inputs.

questions.q: A key question used to appreciate orders of growth is which of the following?
o: How many variables the algorithm declares
How much effect a twofold increase in the input size has on the running time
How many lines of code the algorithm has
Which programming language is fastest
questions.e: One way to appreciate orders of growth is to ask how much effect a twofold (double) increase in the input size has on the algorithm's running time.

questions.q: A brute force approach to solving a problem is best described as which of the following?
o: A clever technique that avoids checking most cases
A straightforward approach based directly on the problem's definition, often checking all possibilities
A method that always transforms the problem first
A method that stores subproblem results in a table
questions.e: Brute force is a straightforward way to solve a problem based on the definition of the problem itself, often involving checking all possibilities (an exhaustive check of all options).

questions.q: Which statement correctly gives a pro of brute force and its main con?
o: Pro: always optimal for large inputs; Con: hard to code
Pro: widely applicable, easy, good for small problem sizes; Con: often inefficient for large inputs
Pro: uses no memory; Con: only works when data is sorted
Pro: fastest known method; Con: cannot be generalised
questions.e: Brute force is widely applicable, easy to implement, and good for small problem sizes, but it is often inefficient for large inputs.

questions.q: Selection sort and bubble sort are cited as brute-force sorts. What is their worst-case time?
o: Θ(n)
Θ(n log n)
questions.e: Both selection sort and bubble sort are brute-force sorting methods, and both take Θ(n^2) time in the worst case.

questions.q: For bubble sort, what are the best-case, worst-case and average-case time complexities?
o: Best O(n), worst O(n^2), average O(n^2)
Best O(n^2), worst O(n^2), average O(n^2)
Best O(1), worst O(n), average O(log n)
Best O(n log n), worst O(n^2), average O(n log n)
questions.e: Bubble sort has best case O(n) (when already sorted, no swaps needed), and worst and average cases O(n^2).

questions.q: For selection sort, what are the best-case, worst-case and average-case time complexities?
o: Best O(n), worst O(n^2), average O(n^2)
All three are O(n^2)
Best O(1), worst O(n^2), average O(n)
All three are O(n log n)
questions.e: Selection sort has best, worst and average case all equal to O(n^2), because it always scans the remaining array to find each successive minimum regardless of the input order.

questions.q: Sequential (linear) search through a list of n items takes what worst-case time?
o: Θ(log n)
Θ(n)
questions.e: A sequential (linear) search goes through the entire list of n items to find the desired one, taking Θ(n) time in the worst case.

questions.q: In linear search, what are the best-case and worst-case numbers of comparisons?
o: Best n, worst 1
Best 1 (found at first position), worst n (found at last position or absent)
Best log n, worst n^2
Best 0, worst n+1
questions.e: Linear search best case is 1 comparison (the element is at the first index, O(1)) and worst case is n comparisons (element at the last index or not present, O(n)). An unsuccessful search takes n+1 comparisons in one formulation.

questions.q: Brute-force graph traversals such as breadth-first search and depth-first search take what time, where V is the number of vertices and E the number of edges?
o: Θ(V)
Θ(E)
Θ(V + E)
Θ(V * E)
questions.e: Both breadth-first search (level by level) and depth-first search (go deep, then backtrack) take Θ(V + E) time, where |V| is the number of vertices and |E| is the number of edges.

questions.q: How is the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) stated?
o: Find the shortest path between two given cities
Given n cities and pairwise distances, find the order to visit every city exactly once and return home with minimum total distance
Sort n cities by their distances
Find the largest distance among all pairs of cities
questions.e: TSP asks, given a set of n cities and the distances between all pairs, to determine the order of travel that visits every city exactly once and returns home with the minimum total distance.

questions.q: The brute-force solution to TSP computes the distance for all tours and chooses the shortest. What is its time complexity?
o: Θ(n)
Θ(n!)
Θ(log n)
questions.e: The brute-force TSP solution computes the distance for all possible tours and picks the shortest, which takes Θ(n!) time — described as terrible because it grows factorially.

questions.q: For a 4-city TSP where the tours and their total distances include a,b,c,d,a = 18; a,b,d,c,a = 11; a,c,d,b,a = 11; and a,c,b,d,a = 23, what is the optimal (minimum) tour distance?
questions.e: Among all the Hamiltonian cycles, the minimum total distance is 11 (achieved by tours such as a,b,d,c,a and a,c,d,b,a), so 11 is the optimal solution.

questions.q: How is the (0-1) Knapsack problem stated for a thief with capacity W?
o: Take the single most valuable item only
Given n items where item i weighs w_i and is worth v_i, and a capacity of W pounds, choose items to maximise total value without exceeding W
Take items until the knapsack is exactly half full
Sort the items by weight and take the lightest
questions.e: In the knapsack problem there are n items, item i weighs w_i pounds and is worth $v_i, and the thief can carry up to W pounds; the goal is to choose what to take to maximise total value.

questions.q: The brute-force solution to the knapsack problem considers every possible subset of items. What is its time complexity?
o: Θ(n)
Θ(n!)
questions.e: The brute-force knapsack solution considers every subset of items, computing each subset's total value and weight and discarding those over W, then choosing the maximum-value feasible subset; this takes Ω(2^n) time.

questions.q: A thief faces items of (weight, value): item1 (7 lb, $42), item2 (3 lb, $12), item3 (4 lb, $40), item4 (5 lb, $25), with capacity W = 10. How many subsets must brute force check, and which is optimal?
o: 8 subsets; optimal {1,2} worth $54
16 subsets; optimal {3,4} weighing 9 lb worth $65
4 subsets; optimal {1} worth $42
10 subsets; optimal {2,3} worth $52
questions.e: With 4 items there are 2^4 = 16 subsets to check. The optimal feasible subset is {3,4}, weighing 4 + 5 = 9 pounds (within W = 10) and worth $40 + $25 = $65.

questions.q: If two algorithms A and B both have the same asymptotic complexity such as O(n^2), will their actual execution times always be equal?
o: Yes, identical asymptotic complexity guarantees identical time
Not necessarily, because asymptotic analysis ignores the constants of proportionality
Yes, but only for large n
No, because O(n^2) is not a valid complexity
questions.e: They may not be equal: there is the matter of the constant of proportionality. If A does ten operations per data item but B does only three, B is reasonably faster even though both are O(n^2), because asymptotic analysis ignores constants of proportionality.

questions.q: Two O(n) algorithms have running times T_A(n) = 50 + 33n and T_B(n) = 200 + 18n. For which inputs is algorithm B the better choice?
o: For all values of n
For values of n > 10
For values of n < 10
Never; A is always better
questions.e: Setting 50 + 33n = 200 + 18n gives n = 10 as the crossover. Algorithm A sets up faster and is better for small n, but for n > 10 algorithm B (which does fewer operations per item) is the better choice.

questions.q: A common misconception links worst-case running time to big-O and best-case to big-Omega. What is the correct relationship?
o: Worst case is defined by big-O and best case by big-Omega, formally
There is no formal relationship; however, worst case and big-O are commonly used together because both find an upper bound
Big-O and worst case are unrelated in every way
Best case is always big-O and worst case big-Omega
questions.e: There is no formal relationship defining worst case by big-O or best case by big-Omega; however, worst case and big-O are commonly used together because they are both techniques for finding an upper bound on running time.

questions.q: In the summary of bubble sort's method, when does the algorithm stop repeating its passes?
o: After exactly one pass through the array
When a pass completes with no swaps performed
When the array is reversed
After n passes regardless of order
questions.e: Bubble sort compares each pair of adjacent elements and swaps them if out of order; it repeats the pass as long as at least one swap was made, and stops when a full pass requires no swaps.

questions.q: In the summary of selection sort's method, what is done on the first step?
o: Swap the first two elements
Find the smallest element in the array and exchange it with the element in the first position
Reverse the whole array
Compare adjacent elements from the end
questions.e: Selection sort finds the smallest element and exchanges it with the element in the first position, then finds the second smallest and places it second, continuing until the array is sorted.

questions.q: Which of the following is given as an application area of the Traveling Salesman Problem?
o: Compiling source code
Drilling printed circuit boards and analysing crystal structure
Encrypting network traffic
Rendering 3-D graphics
questions.e: Applications of TSP include transportation and logistics (school buses, meals on wheels, airplane schedules), drilling printed circuit boards, and analysing crystal structure.

questions.q: The phrase 'exhaustive search' in this context means which of the following?
o: Searching only part of the solution space to save time
An exhaustive check of all possible options without doing anything clever
Searching until the algorithm is exhausted of memory
A search guided by a heuristic
questions.e: Exhaustive search means not doing anything smart — performing an exhaustive check of all possible options, which is the essence of the brute-force approach.

questions.q: Which two algorithms are given as examples of the decrease-and-conquer paradigm?
o: Merge sort and quick sort
Insertion sort and topological sort
Bubble sort and selection sort
Heap sort and radix sort
questions.e: Insertion sort and topological sort are given as examples of the decrease-and-conquer paradigm.

questions.q: Topological sort operates on which kind of input?
o: An undirected weighted graph
A directed acyclic graph (DAG)
A sorted array
A binary search tree
questions.e: Topological sort sorts using a partial order and is provided with a directed acyclic graph (DAG); it runs in linear time.

questions.q: What is the runtime complexity attributed to topological sort?
o: Quadratic
Linear
Logarithmic
Factorial
questions.e: Topological sort has linear runtime complexity.

questions.q: Which of the following is an application of topological sort?
o: Data compression
Course prerequisite scheduling and project management
String matching
Sorting floating-point numbers
questions.e: Applications of topological sort include the course prerequisite scenario and project management, both of which require ordering tasks respecting a partial order.

questions.q: What are the two versions of topological sort?
o: Recursive version and iterative version
Depth-first search version and source-removal version
Top-down version and bottom-up version
Greedy version and dynamic version
questions.e: The two versions of topological sort are the depth-first search version and the source-removal version.

questions.q: In the celebrity problem, how is a celebrity among n people defined?
o: A person who knows everybody and is known by everybody
A person who knows nobody but is known by everybody else
A person who knows exactly one other person
The person who asks the most questions
questions.e: A celebrity among a group of n people is a person who knows nobody but is known by everybody else; the task is to identify the celebrity by only asking questions of the form 'Do you know this person?'.

questions.q: The 'number guessing' (Twenty Questions) puzzle asks you to determine a selected integer in a given range using what kind of questions?
o: Questions that reveal the exact number directly
Questions with yes/no answers
Questions about the number's digits only
Multiple-choice questions
questions.e: In the number guessing (Twenty Questions) puzzle, you determine a selected integer in the range from 1 to n inclusive by asking questions that have yes/no answers.

questions.q: The decrease-and-conquer example of insertion sort builds the result by doing what at each step?
o: Dividing the array into two halves and merging
Taking the next input element and inserting it into its correct place among the already-sorted elements
Selecting the minimum remaining element
Swapping all adjacent out-of-order pairs
questions.e: Insertion sort, a decrease-and-conquer method, maintains a sorted portion and at each step inserts the next input element into its proper place within that sorted portion.

questions.q: Which sorting algorithms are examples of the divide-and-conquer paradigm?
o: Bubble sort and selection sort
Merge sort and quick sort
Insertion sort and topological sort
Counting sort and radix sort
questions.e: Merge sort and quick sort are the two sorting algorithms that serve as examples of the divide-and-conquer paradigm.

questions.q: A divide-and-conquer algorithm divides a problem into subproblems that are of what nature relative to the original?
o: Of a completely different type
Smaller subproblems of the same type, solved recursively
Always exactly two equal halves that are never recombined
Subproblems that require no combination step
questions.e: Divide and conquer divides the problem into smaller subproblems of the same type, solves them recursively, and then combines their solutions into a solution to the original problem.

questions.q: After the subproblems of a divide-and-conquer algorithm are solved recursively, what must happen?
o: The subproblem solutions are discarded
The subproblem solutions are combined into a solution to the original problem
The original problem is re-divided indefinitely
The results are sorted a final time
questions.e: The second essential part of divide and conquer is the combine step: the solutions to the subproblems are combined into a solution to the original problem.

questions.q: Besides merge sort and quick sort, which problem is a divide-and-conquer application?
o: Topological sort
Matrix multiplication
The celebrity problem
Coin change
questions.e: Matrix multiplication is a divide-and-conquer application, in addition to merge sort and quick sort.

questions.q: Merge sort applies the divide-and-conquer strategy by first doing what to the list?
o: Selecting a pivot element
Dividing the list into two parts to be sorted recursively and then merged
Scanning for the smallest element
Building a heap from the list
questions.e: Merge sort, a divide-and-conquer algorithm, divides the list into parts, sorts the parts recursively, and merges the sorted parts together.

questions.q: Quick sort, as a divide-and-conquer method, splits the array around which element?
o: The first element only, always
A pivot element, so that the array is partitioned into parts sorted recursively
The median, which is always known in advance
The largest element
questions.e: Quick sort is a divide-and-conquer algorithm that partitions the array around a pivot element and then recursively sorts the resulting parts.

questions.q: What is the 'mode' of a list of numbers?
o: The average of the numbers
The value that occurs most often in the list
The largest number in the list
The middle value when sorted
questions.e: A mode is a value that occurs most often in a given list of numbers; for example, for 5, 1, 5, 7, 6, 5, 7 the mode is 5. If several values occur most often, any of them can be considered a mode.

questions.q: What is the mode of the list 5, 1, 5, 7, 6, 5, 7?
questions.e: The value 5 appears three times, more than any other value, so the mode of 5, 1, 5, 7, 6, 5, 7 is 5.

questions.q: The brute-force approach to computing the mode works in what way?
o: Sort the list first, then scan once
Scan the list and compute the frequencies of all distinct values, then find the value with the largest frequency
Pick the middle element of the list
Repeatedly halve the list
questions.e: The brute-force mode algorithm scans the list and computes the frequencies of all its distinct values (storing values seen and their counts in an auxiliary list), then finds the value with the largest frequency.

questions.q: For the brute-force mode algorithm that maintains an auxiliary list of distinct values seen, what is the worst-case input?
o: A list where all elements are equal
A list with no equal elements (all distinct)
An already-sorted list
A list of length one
questions.e: The worst-case input for the brute-force mode algorithm is a list with no equal elements, because then the auxiliary list of distinct values grows to full length and every new element is compared against all previous distinct values.

questions.q: What is the transform-and-conquer idea for computing the mode more efficiently?
o: Store all frequencies in a hash table first
Sort the input so equal values become adjacent, then find the longest run of adjacent equal values
Randomly sample the list
Reverse the list and scan it
questions.e: The transform-and-conquer solution first sorts the input so that all equal values are adjacent; the mode is then found as the longest run of adjacent equal values in the sorted array.

questions.q: In the transform-and-conquer mode algorithm, what dominates the running time, and why is its worst case better than the brute-force version?
o: The scanning step; because scanning is slow
The sorting step; with an n log n sort, the overall worst case is in a better asymptotic class than the brute-force algorithm
The comparison step; because comparisons are constant
Nothing dominates; both are identical
questions.e: The running time is dominated by the sorting, since the rest of the algorithm takes linear time; with an n log n sort, this method's worst-case efficiency is in a better asymptotic class than the brute-force algorithm's worst case.

questions.q: The transform-and-conquer strategy, as illustrated by the mode problem, is based on which general idea?
o: Trying every possible option exhaustively
Transforming the problem instance (for example by sorting) into one that is easier to solve
Storing subproblem results in a table
Always making the locally optimal choice
questions.e: Transform and conquer solves a problem by first transforming the instance into a form that is easier to work with — as when the mode problem is solved by transforming the list via sorting so equal values become adjacent.

questions.q: A greedy algorithm works in phases; at each phase it makes what kind of choice?
o: The choice that stores the most information for later
The best choice available right now, without regard for future consequences
A random choice among the options
The choice that leaves the most options open
questions.e: A greedy algorithm works in phases, taking at each phase the best it can get right now without regard for future consequences, hoping that a sequence of local optima leads to a global optimum.

questions.q: What is the difference between a globally optimal and a locally optimal solution?
o: A global optimum is worse than any local optimum
A global optimum has no other feasible solution with a better objective value anywhere; a local optimum has none better only 'in the vicinity'
They are the same thing
A local optimum considers all feasible solutions
questions.e: A globally optimal solution is one for which no other feasible solution has a better objective value; a locally optimal solution is one for which no other feasible solution 'in the vicinity' has a better objective value.

questions.q: How does a greedy strategy typically approach the coin-change problem of paying an amount with the fewest coins?
o: It tries every combination of coins
It repeatedly takes the largest coin that does not exceed the remaining amount
It always takes the smallest coin first
It stores all subresults in a table
questions.e: The greedy coin-change approach repeatedly takes the largest coin that fits within the remaining amount to pay, aiming to use the least number of coins (for example paying 36 from the set 20, 10, 5, 1).

questions.q: In the activity selection problem, how are the activities first processed in the greedy solution?
o: Sorted by start time in ascending order
Sorted by finish time in ascending order, then the first activity is selected
Sorted by duration in descending order
Left unsorted and chosen at random
questions.e: The greedy activity selection sorts the activities by finish time in ascending order, selects the first activity, and then selects each subsequent activity whose start time is greater than or equal to the finish time of the previously selected activity.

questions.q: In greedy activity selection, a new activity is added to the schedule under what condition?
o: Its finish time is earlier than all others
Its start time is greater than or equal to the finish time of the previously selected activity
Its profit is the largest remaining
Its duration is the shortest remaining
questions.e: After selecting the first activity, each new activity is selected only if its starting time is greater than or equal to the finish time of the previously selected activity; this is repeated until all activities are checked.

questions.q: Six activities have (start, finish) times A1(1,2), A2(3,4), A3(0,6), A4(5,7), A5(8,9), A6(5,9). Which set does greedy activity selection choose?
questions.e: Sorting by finish time and greedily choosing non-overlapping activities selects A1 (finish 2), then A2 (start 3 >= 2, finish 4), then A4 (start 5 >= 4, finish 7), then A5 (start 8 >= 7), giving {A1, A2, A4, A5}.

questions.q: In job sequencing with deadlines, the goal is to schedule jobs to do what?
o: Minimise the total number of jobs
Maximise total profit while meeting each scheduled job's deadline
Finish all jobs by the earliest deadline
Sequence jobs in order of arrival
questions.e: Job sequencing with deadlines schedules jobs (each with a profit and a deadline) to maximise total profit, placing jobs so their deadlines are respected; for one instance the selected sequence J6-J7-J4-J3 gives total profit 6+30+20+18 = 74.

questions.q: For jobs with (profit, deadline) J1(20,2), J2(15,2), J3(10,1), J4(5,3), J5(1,3), a greedy job-sequencing solution yields the sequence J1-J2-J4. What total profit does it achieve?
questions.e: Scheduling J1 and J2 in the two slots before deadline 2 and J4 in the slot before deadline 3 gives total profit 20 + 15 + 5 = 40.

questions.q: What is the difference between the 0-1 knapsack problem and the fractional knapsack problem?
o: In 0-1 the thief can take fractions; in fractional he cannot
In 0-1 the items cannot be divided (take an item whole or leave it); in fractional the thief can take partial items
They are identical problems
0-1 allows negative weights; fractional does not
questions.e: In the 0-1 knapsack problem items cannot be divided, so the thief must take an entire item or leave it; in the fractional knapsack problem the thief can take partial items (for example liquids or powders).

questions.q: Which knapsack variant is solvable optimally with a greedy algorithm?
o: The 0-1 knapsack problem
The fractional knapsack problem
Neither variant
Both variants equally
questions.e: The fractional knapsack problem is solvable with a greedy algorithm, whereas the greedy strategy does not guarantee an optimal solution for the 0-1 knapsack problem.

questions.q: In the greedy fractional knapsack algorithm, in what order are items considered?
o: Increasing order of weight
Decreasing order of value per pound (value/weight ratio)
Increasing order of value
The order they are given
questions.e: The greedy fractional knapsack algorithm sorts items in decreasing order of value per pound and, while there is room, takes as much as possible of the next item; the running time is O(n log n), dominated by the sort.

questions.q: What is the running time of the greedy fractional knapsack algorithm, and what dominates it?
o: O(n), dominated by scanning
O(n log n), dominated by the sort of items by value per pound
O(2^n), dominated by trying all subsets
O(n^2), dominated by nested loops
questions.e: The greedy fractional knapsack algorithm runs in O(n log n) time, with the cost dominated by sorting the items in decreasing order of value per pound.

questions.q: Consider a 0-1 knapsack with capacity 50 and items item1(10 lb, $60), item2(20 lb, $100), item3(30 lb, $120). A greedy strategy by value-per-pound takes item1 then item2 and leaves item3. Why is this a problem?
o: The result is optimal, so there is no problem
The greedy choice is suboptimal for 0-1 knapsack; taking item1 looks good locally but is a mistake globally
The knapsack overflows its capacity
The items cannot be compared by value per pound
questions.e: Taking item1 (highest value per pound) then item2 fills the 50-lb knapsack with no room for item3, giving a suboptimal result; taking item1 looks good locally but is a mistake globally, showing greedy does not solve 0-1 knapsack optimally. Dynamic programming can solve it in pseudo-polynomial time.

questions.q: For the fractional knapsack instance with capacity M = 15 and items whose value/weight ratios lead to filling with items 5, 1, 6, 3, 7 fully and item 2 fractionally (2/3), the computed maximum profit is which value?
questions.e: Taking items in decreasing value-per-pound order fills 15 kg using items 5, 1, 6, 3, 7 fully plus 2/3 of item 2, giving a total profit of about 10 + 3.33 + 15 + 6 + 18 + 3 = 55.3.

questions.q: Which technique is noted as able to solve the 0-1 knapsack problem (which greedy cannot solve optimally) in pseudo-polynomial time?
o: Brute force
Dynamic programming
Transform and conquer
Linear search
questions.e: Because the greedy strategy is suboptimal for 0-1 knapsack, dynamic programming is used instead, and it can solve the 0-1 knapsack problem in pseudo-polynomial time.

questions.q: A greedy algorithm is said to hope that a sequence of which choices leads to a global optimum?
o: Randomly chosen options
Local optima chosen at each step
The most expensive options
Exhaustively verified options
questions.e: A greedy algorithm hopes that by choosing a local optimum at each step it will end up at a global optimum, though this is not guaranteed.

questions.q: Compared with dynamic programming, what is stated about the quality and speed of greedy solutions?
o: Greedy always gives the optimal solution more slowly
Greedy usually gives a good/fair solution quickly but does not assure reaching the optimum, whereas dynamic programming gives the optimal solution
Greedy and dynamic programming both guarantee the optimum
Greedy never produces a usable solution
questions.e: Dynamic programming gives the optimal solution, while a greedy algorithm usually gives a good or fair solution in a small amount of time but does not assure that the optimum is reached.

questions.q: Which of the following problems is an application of greedy algorithms?
o: Matrix multiplication
Activity selection
The mode computation
The celebrity problem
questions.e: Problems solved with greedy algorithms include the coin-change problem, activity selection, job sequencing with deadlines, and the fractional knapsack problem.

questions.q: In the activity selection greedy method, after selecting the first activity, how many activities in total are selected for the instance with sets ending in schedule {A1, A2, A4, A5}?
questions.e: The greedy selection for that instance chooses four activities: A1, A2, A4 and A5.

questions.q: For the job-sequencing instance with selected sequence J6-J7-J4-J3, the four chosen jobs have profits 6, 30, 18 and 20. What is the total profit?
questions.e: Summing the profits of the scheduled jobs gives 6 + 30 + 20 + 18 = 74, the total profit for the sequence J6-J7-J4-J3.

questions.q: What are the three elements of a dynamic programming algorithm?
o: Divide, conquer, combine
Sub-problems, table structure, and a bottom-up approach
Sort, scan, select
Guess, check, backtrack
questions.e: The elements of a dynamic programming algorithm are sub-problems, a table structure (to store results), and a bottom-up approach.

questions.q: Dynamic programming is generally applied to which kind of problem?
o: Problems with only one possible solution
Optimization problems where multiple solutions exist and the best must be found
Problems that cannot be broken into subproblems
Problems requiring exhaustive search only
questions.e: A dynamic programming algorithm is generally used for optimization problems, where multiple solutions exist and the goal is to find the best one; it remembers past results and reuses them.

questions.q: The core idea that lets dynamic programming avoid redundant work is that it does what?
o: It discards all intermediate results
It remembers past results and uses them to find new results
It always divides the problem into two equal halves
It makes a single greedy choice at each step
questions.e: A dynamic programming algorithm remembers past results and uses them to find new results, which is why a table structure is one of its elements.

questions.q: Storing the results of sub-problems in a table so they are computed only once is characteristic of which element of dynamic programming?
o: The bottom-up approach
The table structure
The divide step
The greedy choice
questions.e: The table structure is the dynamic programming element responsible for storing the solutions to sub-problems, so that each sub-problem's result is available for reuse rather than recomputed.

questions.q: How does the bottom-up approach in dynamic programming build a solution?
o: By starting from the full problem and recursing downward without storing results
By solving and storing the smallest sub-problems first and combining them upward toward the full problem
By making a locally optimal choice at each step
By trying all subsets exhaustively
questions.e: The bottom-up approach, one of the elements of dynamic programming, solves the smallest sub-problems first, stores their results in the table, and builds up toward the solution of the full problem.

questions.q: How does dynamic programming differ from a greedy method when solving a problem such as finding a best route through intermediate places?
o: Dynamic programming goes only to the nearest place; greedy tries all places
Dynamic programming tries all the places but stores previous results, whereas greedy just goes to the nearest place at each step
Both try all places and store results
Neither stores any results
questions.e: In the route illustration, the greedy method goes to the nearest intermediate place at each step, while dynamic programming tries all the places but stores the previous results for reuse, which lets it find the optimal solution.
